Mohandas Gandhi. The spiritual leader of India's independence struggle and pioneer of nonviolent resistance, shot and killed on January 30, 1948, just months after India gained independence from British rule.

Gandhi was shot in Delhi at Birla House, the home of his host, by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist extremist. Godse fired three bullets at close range, and Gandhi died within minutes. His final words were reportedly "Hai Ram," meaning "Oh God." The assassination happened during the Hindu festival of Holi, a time of celebration darkened by the killing.

Godse opposed Gandhi's message of Hindu-Muslim unity and blamed him for Pakistan's creation. He belonged to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, a paramilitary Hindu nationalist organization. India had gained independence just months earlier in August 1947, and the partition into India and Pakistan had triggered massive communal violence between Hindus and Muslims. Gandhi had responded by fasting and preaching nonviolence and harmony, which infuriated Hindu extremists.

Gandhi had survived earlier assassination attempts and refused personal security, believing absolutely in his cause. Yet the conspirators felt their grievances were justified. Godse was tried, convicted, and executed in 1949. The RSS was banned temporarily.

Gandhi's death unified India in grief and shocked the world, elevating his moral status internationally. The assassination became a tragic irony: the man who had wielded nonviolence as a weapon against an empire was cut down by violence rooted in religious nationalism. His refusal of protection was consistent with his philosophy but made him vulnerable to zealots. In global memory, Gandhi's death became inseparable from his life—the final testament to his beliefs. He shares a connection to India's independence, to Jawaharlal Nehru who became his political heir after independence, and to the philosophy of nonviolent resistance that he pioneered and died defending.
